content:
I am porting a formally verified compiler from HOL to Lean. The source language Pancake is a rather low-level programming language without undefined behaviors; this can be compiled down to machine code without garbage collection.

The Lean port is called Flapjack because somebody (who lives in England) told me Flapjack means Pancake in English.

Today my bots finished porting the compiler correctness theorem from Pancake [edit: AST] to RISC-V backend. The rough intended statement is: if the source terminates with output, the machine code also terminates with the same output. The statements are huge in HOL and in Lean, and I want to stare at them more.

Another big hole is: the RISC-V semantics has not been validated in any way. Comparison with Sail RISC-V model is future work.

I have a speculation that Iris-Lean might help extending this to support concurrency. Also, a proof checker in Flapjack might help reducing trust on compilers.

[edit: proof starts with Pancake AST after parsing and a conversion.]

The RISC-V semantics in Flapjack differs from the authoritative Sail RISC-V in certain ways: https://github.com/flamingoponderado/flapjack-riscv-check . My current plan is that Flapjack (at least the main branch) will be following the original Pancake's choices.
I very much appreciate the disclaimer at the top of the page and the "small print" at the end. I mean this genuinely, it's refreshing to see this straightforwardly stated.

The statement of the main theorem spans 53 lines. It's freshly vibe-ported. What do I know.

I'm trying one concrete example now. Maybe I'll be able to satisfy all the assumptions at the same time.

The concrete example involved proving 'compile src = bytecode'. src AST is roughly 3 MB. The proof of the equality occupies 56,000 Lean files totalling 2.12 GB. It builds but I haven't seen the comparator finishing. I'm avoiding native_decide. I guess I'm hitting the performance issue that motivated cv_compute in HOL4.
